evidence_snippets: “In the absence of natural boosting, data indicate that immunity following a 3-dose primary vaccination schedule wanes over time. Therefore, booster doses are needed to ensure continuing protection.”

“Data on the duration of seroprotection from 2 large representative population studies from the Netherlands, using a complete 3-dose primary series plus 3-dose booster series prior to adolescence, indicate that this schedule results in very high seroprevalence above the threshold for basic protection (≥0.01 IU/mL) up to 39 years of age and potentially longer.”
“A seroprevalence of 94.6% (95% CI: 87.3–100%) for basic protection was observed even in the age group 35–39 years.”
“A seroprevalence of 37.8% (95% CI: 22.2–53.5%) above the threshold for full protection (0.1 IU/mL) was observed in the age group 35–39 years.”
“These data indicate that following a 3-dose primary plus 3-dose booster schedule, administration of decennial booster doses may not be necessary through middle age.”

“Among women who had received a complete DTP-containing primary series (3 doses) in Portugal during childhood and at least one booster (n=22), none were found to be susceptible before 25 years had elapsed since the last dose.”
“All those who had received at least 6 doses (n=17) had anti-diphtheria antibody levels above the threshold for full protection up to 38 years since the last dose.”
“A cross-sectional seroprevalence study in one State in the USA modelled a half-life for diphtheria-specific immunity (>0.01 IU/mL) of 27 years (95% CI: 18–51 years).”
“No evidence could be retrieved on the duration of protective immunity following a 3-dose primary vaccination series in adults.”

“Among children infected with HIV type 1 (HIV-1), 70.8% developed protective antibody titres following diphtheria toxoid administered at 6, 10, and 14 weeks compared with 98.5% among HIV-1 negative children (P < 0.05). Geometric mean antibody titres to diphtheria were significantly lower in children with HIV-1 infection than in uninfected children.”

“Multiple linear regression analysis showed lower diphtheria antibody levels, independent of the interval between last booster and antibody assessment, in HIV-1 infected women than in uninfected women. Following a booster dose the mean diphtheria antibody levels were higher in uninfected than in HIV-infected women.”
“As responses to booster vaccination can still be elicited after intervals of 25–30 years, it is not necessary to repeat a primary vaccination series when booster doses have been delayed.”
key_data_points: Waning: immunity after 3-dose primary series wanes over time in absence of natural boosting; boosters needed
Netherlands (3-dose primary + 3 boosters pre-adolescence): seroprevalence ≥0.01 IU/mL up to 39 years and potentially longer
Netherlands age 35–39: 94.6% (95% CI 87.3–100%) ≥0.01 IU/mL (basic protection)
Netherlands age 35–39: 37.8% (95% CI 22.2–53.5%) ≥0.1 IU/mL (full protection)
Portugal women (3-dose primary + ≥1 booster; n=22): none susceptible before 25 years since last dose
Portugal women with ≥6 doses (n=17): antibody levels above full protection threshold up to 38 years since last dose
USA cross-sectional model: half-life of diphtheria-specific immunity (>0.01 IU/mL) 27 years (95% CI 18–51)
Adults: no evidence retrieved on duration of protective immunity after 3-dose primary series
HIV-1 infected children: 70.8% developed protective titres after 6,10,14-week schedule vs 98.5% in HIV-negative (P<0.05); lower GMTs
HIV-1 infected women: lower diphtheria antibody levels than uninfected; booster increases levels but remains higher in uninfected
study_population: General population serosurveys (Netherlands; UK; Singapore; USA state) and adult women in Portugal; special risk group data in HIV-1 infected children and HIV-1 infected women

evidence_snippets: “However, immunity declines with time. One year after vaccination, the percentage of poorly-protected persons may increase to 20% and the mean titre may fall to the protective threshold.”

“In a study in pregnant women with no previous tetanus vaccination, 78% of those who received 2 doses during pregnancy had tetanus-specific antibody levels above the protective threshold 3 years later.”
“After the third dose, each additional dose given with an interval of at least a 1 year increases the tetanus-specific antibody levels and prolongs the duration of immunity.”
“Data from serological studies suggest that a primary series of 3 TTCV doses in infancy plus a booster during the second year of life will provide 3–5 years of protection.”

“In the Netherlands, results from use of a 6-dose schedule of TTCVs in childhood with the last dose at 8 years of age demonstrated that tetanus immunity persisted for at least 20 years after the sixth dose, with a geometric mean titre (GMT) of 0.44 IU/ml in individuals aged 30–34 years. A regression analysis from this serological data predicted that protective antibody levels would persist until 90 years of age, with a GMT of 0.22 IU/ml.”

“In two studies that evaluated immune persistence at 4–6 years of age following 4 doses of TTCV, 75% and 76% of children continued to have seroprotective antibody levels against tetanus approximately 3.5 years after boosting.”

“In one of these studies, at 7–9 years of age 65% of children who were not further vaccinated had protective tetanus-specific antibody levels compared to 100% of those who received a booster dose at age 5–6 years.”
“Booster responses can still be elicited after intervals of 25–30 years, demonstrating the persistence of immunological memory.”
“Ten years after immunization, tetanus antibody levels still exceeded pre-immunization levels and remained protective (≥0.10 IU/ml) in ≥97% of adolescents and adults.”
“Immunity gaps may exist in the elderly due to waning immunity or non-vaccination, especially among females (elderly males were generally vaccinated during military service).”
key_data_points: Waning: 1 year after vaccination, up to 20% may be poorly protected; mean titre may fall to protective threshold
Pregnant women (previously unvaccinated): 78% above protective threshold at 3 years after 2 doses during pregnancy
Children: 3-dose infancy series + booster in 2nd year of life provides 3–5 years of protection
Netherlands serology (6-dose schedule; last dose at 8y): immunity persisted ≥20 years after 6th dose; GMT 0.44 IU/ml at age 30–34; predicted persistence until 90y with GMT 0.22 IU/ml
Hexavalent-related persistence: at age 4–6y after 4 TTCV doses, 75% and 76% seroprotected ~3.5 years after booster
At age 7–9y: 65% seroprotected without further vaccination vs 100% with booster at 5–6y
Immunological memory: booster responses elicited after 25–30 year intervals
Adolescents/adults: 10 years post-immunization, ≥97% remained protective (≥0.10 IU/ml)
study_population: General population across age groups (infants/children, adolescents/adults, pregnant women); includes evidence from serological studies in the USA and the Netherlands and studies of hexavalent vaccine schedules; notes on elderly as a risk group

evidence_snippets: “Waning of vaccine-derived protection and reduced boosting of immunity by circulating B. pertussis are likely to increase the susceptibility of adolescents and adults.”

“An observational study of pertussis attack rates in a general practice community in the UK showed that wP vaccine effectiveness fell from 100% in the first year after the primary vaccination to 84% in the 4th year, 52% in the 5th year and to 46% in the 6th year.”
“Duration of immunity acquired after a 3p series of wP vaccine is estimated to range from 4 to 12 years.”
“For the vaccines currently in use, the 2014 systematic review indicates a maximum annual loss of protection of 13% and a minimum loss of 2% following a primary vaccination series.”

“A large study in Italy of 2 aP-containing vaccines 6 years after completion of the primary immunization series in children (with a 2, 4, 6 month schedule) showed protective efficacies of 76% and 85%, respectively, using 2 clinical definitions of pertussis of differing specificity.”
“In Sweden, a 2-dose primary aP immunization series with a booster at age 12 months provided protection against pertussis for approximately 5 years.”
“There is now increasing evidence that protection following booster doses of aP vaccines wanes faster in individuals primed with aP rather than with wP vaccines.”
“Epidemiological data show waning immunity in school-aged children, adolescents and young adults in populations receiving aP vaccine.”

“These data suggest that when aP-containing vaccines are used in low-incidence settings, a 3-dose primary series and a booster in the second year of life may provide insufficient protection for children aged >6 years; thus, these doses should be followed by an additional booster dose administered at the time of school entry.”

“Data also suggest a faster waning of protection following repeated booster doses. In contrast, wP vaccine used for at least the 1st dose provides longer-lasting protection irrespective of the subsequent doses.”

“Although these programmes (other than vaccination of pregnant women) have an impact in the directly targeted populations, there is as yet no substantial evidence that they have had a significant impact on severe pertussis in infants; they are possibly of limited impact because of the more rapid waning of immunity observed after aP vaccination relative to the duration of immunity after wP vaccination.”
“This schedule should provide protection for at least 6 years for countries using wP vaccine. For countries using aP vaccine, protection may decline appreciably before 6 years of age.”
key_data_points: wP effectiveness over time (UK observational study): 100% (year 1) → 84% (year 4) → 52% (year 5) → 46% (year 6) after primary vaccination
Estimated duration of immunity after 3-dose primary (wP, 3p): 4–12 years
Annual loss of protection after primary series (2014 systematic review): maximum 13% per year; minimum 2% per year
aP protective efficacy at 6 years post-primary series (Italy; schedule 2,4,6 months): 76% and 85% (two clinical definitions)
aP 2-dose primary + booster at 12 months (Sweden): protection for ~5 years
Programmatic statement: protection for at least 6 years with wP schedules; with aP, protection may decline appreciably before 6 years
study_population: General populations across age groups (children, school-aged children, adolescents, young adults); specific cited studies include children in the UK general practice community, children in Italy (6 years post-primary series), and children in Sweden (2-dose primary + booster at 12 months).

evidence_snippets: “An anti-HBs antibody concentration of ≥10 mIU/mL measured 1-2 months after administration of the last dose of the primary vaccination series is considered a reliable serological marker of long-term protection against HBV infection.”

“In these studies, 3-dose schedules commonly resulted in higher concentrations of anti-HBs antibody 1–3 months post-vaccination, and more prolonged persistence of anti-HBs antibody, compared to 2-dose schedules.”

“In a study in Alaska, USA, which is an intermediate endemic area, a 3-dose vaccination schedule (second dose after 1 month, third dose after 6 months) with a plasma-derived hepatitis B vaccine in a cohort of 1578 uninfected persons aged 6 months to 50 years prevented all clinically apparent and chronic HBV infection for at least 30 years.”
“Among a subset of the cohort (243 subjects) that had not received booster vaccination, 49% had anti-HBs antibody titres of <10 mIU/mL at 30 years.”
“Most (88%) persons without this seroprotective level of anti-HBs antibody responded with a rapid rise in titre after a booster dose, indicating immunologic memory and persistence of protection.”

“From these data, it was estimated that approximately 90% (range 74%–100%) of vaccinees remained protected for at least 30 years, irrespective of the presence or absence of measurable anti-HBs antibody.”

“In other long-term follow-up studies after neonatal vaccination, protection against HBV infection was maintained even though about two thirds of vaccinees had anti-HBs antibody levels <10 mIU/mL after 30 years.”

“A review and meta-analysis of 22 studies including 11 090 persons 5–20 years after vaccination found no chronic HBV infection, although the cumulative incidence of subclinical HBV infection (transient or persistent anti-HBc antibody) was 0.7% (95% CI: 0.5%–1.0%); it was concluded that individuals adequately vaccinated in a 3-dose or 4-dose schedule do not require a booster dose.”
“In other cohorts monitored for 20 years or longer subclinical infection rates of 1%–27% among vaccinees were reported.”
“There is no evidence of a difference in protection with or without a booster dose administered when anti-HBs antibody concentrations decline to <10 mIU/mL.”

“The majority of previously vaccinated people whose anti-HBs antibody concentration decreases to <10 mIU/mL mount an anamnestic response when they receive a booster dose or exposure to HBV, indicating that they remained protected by memory T-cells.”

“Additional long-term studies are needed to explore lifelong protection conferred by hepatitis B vaccine and the need for booster doses in different subgroups of the population, particularly in HIV-infected/HIV-exposed infants.”

“In a 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis addressing the immune responses among HIV-positive individuals to hepatitis B vaccine with standard versus high dosage, 6 studies among adults found higher peak anti-HBs antibody titres after the higher dosage compared to the standard dosage vaccines but no clear difference in the proportion of adults with protective antibodies up to 5 years after vaccination.”
“In 6 other studies among children, use of double dosage compared to standard dosage protocols did not improve the duration of seroprotection 2–5 years after vaccination.”
“This vaccine may elicit an earlier, higher and more long-lasting antibody response than a corresponding series of 4 double doses (40 µg) of standard hepatitis B vaccine.”
key_data_points: Seroprotection threshold: anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL (measured 1–2 months after last primary dose) considered marker of long-term protection
Duration of protection: prevented all clinically apparent and chronic HBV infection for at least 30 years (Alaska cohort; 3-dose schedule)
Waning antibodies: 49% had anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL at 30 years (subset without boosters)
Anamnestic response: 88% of those with anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL responded rapidly to booster (immunologic memory)
Estimated protection: ~90% (range 74%–100%) protected for at least 30 years irrespective of measurable anti-HBs
Neonatal vaccination follow-up: ~two thirds had anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL after 30 years, yet protection maintained
Meta-analysis (5–20 years post-vaccination; n=11,090): no chronic HBV infection; subclinical infection cumulative incidence 0.7% (95% CI 0.5%–1.0%)
Long-term cohorts (≥20 years): subclinical infection rates reported 1%–27%
HIV-positive adults: no clear difference in proportion with protective antibodies up to 5 years after vaccination (high vs standard dose)
HIV-positive children: double vs standard dose did not improve duration of seroprotection 2–5 years after vaccination
study_population: General populations vaccinated against hepatitis B (including long-term follow-up cohorts such as Alaska cohort aged 6 months–50 years; neonatal vaccination cohorts); and risk groups including HIV-positive adults and children, and patients with renal insufficiency/haemodialysis (booster/long-lasting response statements).

evidence_snippets: “Field studies set a threshold of 1μg/ml, one month after completion of the primary vaccination series, as the level required to confer long-term protection from invasive Hib disease.”

“Although there is some evidence of a decrease over time in the proportion of Hib vaccine recipients with antibody levels higher than the set thresholds, there is only limited evidence to suggest that this decline is associated with an increase in clinical disease.”

“After successfully controlling Hib disease with a 3-dose primary schedule, a few countries have reported small increases in incidence, but these are much lower than levels seen in the pre-vaccine era.”

“However, such resurgences may not occur until many years after vaccine introduction, as was observed in the United Kingdom where resurgence in invasive Hib disease was reported after a decade of successful Hib control, requiring the introduction of a booster dose.”

“There is currently insufficient information to determine whether or not there is a need for a booster dose, which may be influenced by local epidemiology, co-administered vaccines, and the potential for natural boosting as well as other factors.”

“A recent evaluation from 4 South American countries reported that Hib meningitis rates were similar 6–10 years after introduction of the vaccine in countries where booster doses were used and in those where boosters were not used.”

“Limited evidence (mainly from South Africa) suggests that HIV-infected children would benefit from receiving a booster dose regardless of the number of primary doses received and regardless of anti-retroviral therapy.”
key_data_points: Long-term protection correlate: anti-PRP IgG ≥1 μg/ml measured 1 month after completion of primary series
Waning: evidence of decreasing proportion above antibody thresholds over time; limited evidence linking this to increased clinical disease
Resurgence timing: United Kingdom resurgence reported after ~10 years of successful control; booster dose introduced
Post-introduction disease persistence: Hib meningitis rates similar 6–10 years after introduction in 4 South American countries (booster vs no booster)
Risk group: HIV-infected children may benefit from a booster dose regardless of primary series/ART
study_population: General infant/child populations in countries using Hib conjugate vaccines (including developing countries; 4 South American countries; United Kingdom); special risk group: HIV-infected children (evidence mainly from South Africa)

evidence_snippets: “Active immunity induced either by vaccination or exposure to poliovirus (usually measured by level of circulating antibody titres), provides lifelong protection against paralytic disease.”
“However, as antibody titres decline over time and may fall below detectable levels, seroprevalence may not reflect the true immune status of a given population.”

“While seroconversion is a reliable correlate of immunity against paralytic disease, there is no evidence that loss of detectable antibody places immunocompetent individuals at risk for paralytic poliomyelitis.”

“A cross sectional survey conducted in Gambia documented that children aged 3–4 years who received 3 tOPV doses through routine immunization still had detectable antibodies to poliovirus types 1 (88.1%) and 3 (89.3%).”

“A similar study in Sri Lanka which tested children aged 9–11 months, 3–4 years, 7–9 years, and 15 years, found >95% children were seropositive for poliovirus types 1 and 2 in all age groups; for type 3, the seropositivity rates were 95%, 90%, 77% and 75% for the 4 respective age groups.”

“Mucosal immunity induced by OPV vaccination in India was demonstrated to wane significantly within 1 year of vaccination, contingent on factors influencing mucosal response including when the last OPV dose was received, the number of OPV doses received, and seasonality correlated to enteric virus exposure.”
“Information from high-income countries on the duration of IPV-induced protection indicates that circulating antibody persists for decades and possibly for life.”
“Persisting neutralizing antibodies against polioviruses are usually found in all vaccine recipients 5 years after a primary immunization series of 3–4 doses.”
“However, the usual decline of antibody titres over time may result in a high proportion of individuals becoming seronegative a few years after vaccination.”

“In Pakistan, the decline in antibody titres 12 months following 2 doses of IPV at 14 weeks and 9 months was similar for both full dose IPV and fIPV recipients: seroprevalence of poliovirus type 2 antibodies at age 10 months was 100% and 99% (p=0.339), and at 21 months, 86% and 67% (p=0.004) for IPV and ID fIPV respectively.”
“OPV vaccination of individuals with PID can lead to paralysis and persistent (>6 months to 5 years), or chronic (>5 years) shedding of iVDPV strains.”
key_data_points: Active immunity (vaccination or exposure): lifelong protection against paralytic disease (qualitative statement)
Gambia (3–4 years after 3 tOPV doses): detectable antibodies PV1 88.1%, PV3 89.3%
Sri Lanka seropositivity by age group (9–11 months / 3–4 years / 7–9 years / 15 years): PV1 & PV2 >95% in all age groups; PV3 95%, 90%, 77%, 75%
OPV mucosal immunity: wanes significantly within 1 year (India) (qualitative statement)
IPV-induced circulating antibody: persists for decades and possibly for life (qualitative statement)
Neutralizing antibodies: usually found in all recipients 5 years after 3–4 dose primary series (qualitative statement)
Pakistan IPV vs ID fIPV (PV2 seroprevalence): 10 months 100% vs 99% (p=0.339); 21 months 86% vs 67% (p=0.004)
Risk group (primary immunodeficiency): persistent shedding >6 months to 5 years; chronic shedding >5 years (iVDPV)
study_population: General populations receiving OPV/IPV (including children in Gambia and Sri Lanka; infants/children in India for mucosal waning; children in Pakistan for antibody persistence); risk group: individuals with primary immunodeficiency disorders (PID) with prolonged poliovirus shedding after OPV

evidence_snippets: “A review of the published data on duration of immunity reveals estimates that infection-acquired immunity against pertussis disease wanes after 4–20 years and protective immunity after vaccination wanes after 4–12 years.”
“The current estimates of the duration of infection-acquired immunity range from 7–10 years … to 20 years.”
“This study provided well-documented evidence that the duration of infection-acquired immunity in children may be as short as 3.5 years.”
“The mean time between the first and second infections was 7.1 years … in the unvaccinated children and 5.1 years … in the previously vaccinated children.”
“Estimates of the duration of immunity acquired after wP vaccination range from 4 to 12 years.”
“[Lambert] … demonstrating that 95% of the attacks had occurred within 12 years since the last dose of wP vaccine.”
“He estimated that by 4 years after immunization, only 52% of the children still had a clinically protective level of immunity against pertussis.”
“This study thus provides evidence that immunity acquired by wP vaccination wanes 6–9 years after the last dose.”
“A prospective surveillance study … demonstrated sustained efficacy of 86% for typical pertussis and 76–78% for mild pertussis during the first 6 years of life (ie, >5 years after the last dose).”
“In a Swedish 10-year follow-up study, 13% of the study population acquired pertussis infection, with a median age of 5.5 years after the last dose, irrespective of type of vaccine.”
“In a German 6-year follow-up study … the calculated efficacy for the 6-year follow-up period was 89% (95% CI 79–94) for the aP vaccine and 92% (95% CI 84–96) for the wP vaccine.”
“By ~2 years postinfection or postvaccination with either wP or aP vaccine, antibodies have reached barely detectable levels, whereas immunity against infection remains.”

“Protective immunity after infection was probably never lifelong and wanes after 7–20 years. Duration of immunity after either wP or aP immunization does not appear to substantially differ and likely lasts 4–12 years in children.”
key_data_points: Infection-acquired immunity wanes: 4–20 years (also stated 7–20 years; 7–10 years to 20 years)
In children, infection-acquired immunity may be as short as 3.5 years (Netherlands cohort reinfections)
Mean interval between first and second confirmed infections (Senegal): 7.1 years (unvaccinated) vs 5.1 years (previously vaccinated)
Whole-cell pertussis (wP) vaccine duration estimates: 4–12 years
Outbreak data: 95% of attacks occurred within 12 years since last wP dose
Community study estimate: by 4 years after immunization, 52% still had clinically protective immunity
Australian notifications suggest waning 6–9 years after last wP dose
Acellular pertussis (aP) sustained efficacy: 86% typical pertussis and 76–78% mild pertussis during first 6 years of life (>5 years after last dose)
Swedish 10-year follow-up: 13% acquired infection; median 5.5 years after last dose (regardless of vaccine type)
German 6-year follow-up efficacy: aP 89% (95% CI 79–94) vs wP 92% (95% CI 84–96)
Antibodies barely detectable by ~2 years postinfection/postvaccination, though immunity against infection remains
study_population: Review of published studies on pertussis immunity duration after natural infection and after whole-cell (wP) or acellular (aP) pertussis vaccination; includes children and household/community populations from multiple countries (e.g., Netherlands, Senegal, Australia, Sweden, Germany, U.S., U.K.).

evidence_snippets: “After each subsequent dose of vaccine, immunity is boosted, then persists above the protective threshold for a time, and then wanes over time.”
“Putatively protective levels of immunity are induced by a primary series of three TTCV doses and immunity typically persists for at least 5 years.”
“Immunity may persist for approximately 10 years after the fourth dose of TTCV and for at least 20 years after the fifth dose.”
“In summary, a primary series of 3 TTCV doses in infancy plus a booster during the second year of life will provide 3-5 years of protection.”
“Booster responses after 6 TTCVs can be elicited after intervals of 20-30 years.”

“Although the half-life of tetanus immunity has been estimated to be approximately 11 years, other evidence suggests that antibody levels decline significantly over a 10-year period following the peak at 1 month post-vaccination.”

“In the absence of recommendations for adult TTCV boosters or when recommendations are made but uptake is suboptimal, a proportion of older adults, which will vary by setting, may experience significant waning of immunity resulting in antibody levels below putatively protective thresholds.”

“Analysis of the antibody levels of 439 participants who received three doses of TT at these later ages without being revaccinated suggested that antibody levels persisted above 0.1 IU/mL (by ELISA) up to 25 years after the last immunization.”

“The authors concluded that this schedule of primary immunization in infancy gives approximately 5 years of protection and that revaccination within 5 years of the last dose induces immunity for up to approximately 20 years.”

“Data from a cross-sectional study in the Netherlands, where six doses of TT are given in childhood and the final dose is provided at 9 years of age, also demonstrated that at approximately 20 years after the last dose the geometric mean antibody level was 0.44 IU/mL by the ToBI assay.”

“A study in Papua New Guinea showed that 78% of women immunized during pregnancy with two doses of adsorbed TT containing 10 Lf had antitoxin levels above 0.01 IU/ml for at least three years as measured by neutralization; the mean antitoxin level was about 0.03 IU/ml.”
“For tetanus antitoxin, the half-life of maternal antibody was found to be 43–57 days.”

“Among HIV-positive children and adults, the proportion of HIV-positive persons who respond to TTCVs is similar to the proportion of HIV-uninfected individuals, though responses are often lower and may wane more quickly.”
key_data_points: Primary series (3 TTCV doses): immunity typically persists for at least 5 years
After 4th TTCV dose: immunity may persist ~10 years
After 5th TTCV dose: immunity persists at least 20 years
3 TTCV doses in infancy + booster in 2nd year of life: 3–5 years of protection
Booster responses after 6 TTCVs can be elicited after 20–30 year intervals
Half-life of tetanus immunity estimated ~11 years; antibody levels decline significantly over 10 years post-peak (1 month post-vaccination)

Denmark (3-dose schedule, no revaccination): antibody levels persisted >0.1 IU/mL (ELISA) up to 25 years after last immunization; primary immunization gives ~5 years protection; revaccination within 5 years induces immunity up to ~20 years
Netherlands (6 childhood doses; last at 9 years): ~20 years after last dose, GMC 0.44 IU/mL (ToBI)
Pregnant women (Papua New Guinea) after 2 doses adsorbed TT: 78% had antitoxin >0.01 IU/mL for at least 3 years; mean ~0.03 IU/mL (neutralization)
Maternal tetanus antibody half-life in infants: 43–57 days
Risk group: HIV-positive individuals—responses often lower and may wane more quickly
study_population: General population across life course (infants/children/adolescents/adults) receiving tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccines (including combination vaccines such as hexavalent); includes risk groups noted (older adults with waning immunity; HIV-positive children/adults; pregnant women and infants with maternally-derived antibodies).

evidence_snippets: Persons were tested for antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs) levels 30 years after receiving the primary series.
Among 243 persons (56%) who responded to the original primary series but received no subsequent doses during the 30-year period, 125 (51%) had an anti-HBs level ≥10 mIU/mL.
After 22 years, 60% had a protective level of antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs; ≥10 mIU/mL), and overall 93% seemed to be protected (had antibody and/or responded to booster dose).
Among participants with anti-HBs levels <10 mIU/mL who were available for follow-up, 75 of 85 (88%) responded to a booster dose with an anti-HBs level ≥10 mIU/mL at 30 days.
Among the 63 study participants in group 3, only 9 (14%) had anti-HBs levels ≥10 mIU/mL 8 years after their booster dose, and the GMC of anti-HBs was 3.6 mIU/mL.

This study... is the longest cohort study on long-term protection after hepatitis B vaccination... It shows that protection from the vaccine continues out to 30 years; ≥94% of persons had evidence of protection (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL or response to booster dose of vaccine).

Among participants in groups 1 and 2 with an anti-HBs level <10 mIU/mL at 30 years, those with a higher preboost anti-HBs level were more likely to demonstrate a booster response (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL) than those with lower preboost anti-HBs levels. This suggests that even if the anti-HBs level at 30 years has waned to <10 mIU/mL, the closer the level is to 10 mIU/mL, the higher the probability that the boost will succeed.

Our study provides strong evidence to support the CDC recommendation that protection, after a complete series of hepatitis B vaccine and documentation of the initial response, will last for ≥30 years.
key_data_points: Follow-up duration: 30 years after primary hepatitis B vaccination series
Protective antibody (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL) at 30 years: 219/435 (50%) overall
Group 1 (no 22-year participation; primary responders, no subsequent doses): anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL at 30 years: 125/243 (51%); GMC 14.4 mIU/mL
22-year follow-up: 60% had anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL; overall 93% protected (antibody and/or booster response)
Booster response at 30 years (group 1, anti-HBs <10): 75/85 (88%) achieved anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL at 30 days; GMC 150.4 mIU/mL
Group 2 booster response at 30 years (anti-HBs <10): 33/36 (92%) achieved anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL at 30 days; GMC 419.8 mIU/mL
Estimated evidence of protection at 30 years among primary responders (anti-HBs ≥10 or booster response): 94% (applying 88% booster response to those with anti-HBs <10)
Waning after booster: 8 years after booster (given at 22 years), anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL: 9/63 (14%); GMC 3.6 mIU/mL
No new breakthrough infections observed at 30 years
study_population: Alaska Native adults and children aged ≥6 months at primary vaccination in 1981 (plasma-derived hepatitis B vaccine, 3-dose series); subset followed up 30 years later (2011) from 12 Alaska communities, including those who moved to Anchorage/Bethel; primary-series responders with no additional doses (except a subgroup boosted at 22 years).

evidence_snippets: Blood samples were collected to evaluate the persistence of hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) at 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 years of age.
The results showed that at 7 years of age, a higher percentage of children in the hexavalent group maintained anti-HBs levels ≥ 10 mIU/mL compared to those in the pentavalent group (86.9% vs. 59.7%).
This study showed good persistence of anti-HBs among hexavalent-vaccinated children 5.5 years after the last dose of the HepB vaccine.

Although anti-HBs levels waned over time, the hexavalent group demonstrated higher anti-HBs GMCs (approximately by one log scale) at each time point after booster, compared to the pentavalent and EPI pentavalent groups (Fig. 1).
The percentages of children with seroprotective concentration decreased over time, as illustrated in Table 1.

In terms of seroprotection rate, anti-HBs levels ≥ 10 mIU/mL were achieved in 100 % of the children in the hexavalent group, 99.2 % in the pentavalent group and 93.8 % of those in the EPI pentavalent group one month after the booster.

Nevertheless, a significantly higher proportion of children in the hexavalent group maintained anti-HBs levels ≥ 10 mIU/mL compared to the pentavalent and EPI pentavalent groups at 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 years of age.

The primary objective of the current study is to assess the persistence of anti-HBs up to the age of seven, which corresponds to 5.5 years post-administration of the last HepB vaccination dose...
key_data_points: Follow-up duration: anti-HBs measured at ages 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 years (months 36, 48, 60, 72, 84), corresponding to ~5.5 years after last HepB dose (booster at 18 months).
Seroprotection threshold: anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL.
Seroprotection at 7 years (month 84): Hexavalent 86.9% (80/92) vs Pentavalent 59.7% (46/77) vs EPI pentavalent 48.8% (21/43).
Seroprotection over time (hexavalent): 95.8% (3y), 95.0% (4y), 92.5% (5y), 90.1% (6y), 86.9% (7y).
Seroprotection over time (pentavalent): 71.2% (3y), 69.7% (4y), 61.7% (5y), 60.9% (6y), 59.7% (7y).
Seroprotection over time (EPI pentavalent): 68.4% (3y), 61.8% (4y), 54.2% (5y), 47.8% (6y), 48.8% (7y).
Waning: 'anti-HBs levels waned over time' and 'percentages... decreased over time'.
Anti-HBs GMC at 7 years (month 84): Hexavalent 143.2 mIU/mL (95% CI 93.4–219.6) vs Pentavalent 14.8 (9.6–22.7) vs EPI pentavalent 9.6 (5.3–17.3).
study_population: Healthy full-term and late preterm children in Bangkok, Thailand, who received monovalent HepB at birth plus either hexavalent (Infanrix hexa) or pentavalent (Quinvaxem) vaccines at 2, 4, 6 months and booster at 18 months; plus an additional EPI pentavalent comparison cohort.

evidence_snippets: “Blood samples were collected for evaluation of antibody persistence to diphtheria toxoid (DT), tetanus toxoid (TT), and Bordetella pertussis (B. pertussis) between 2 and 6 y of age annually… Antibody persistence to Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) was followed until 3 y of age.”
“Before the second booster, we observed a decrease in anti-DT IgG (Figure 2a) and anti-TT IgG (Figure 2b) from month 19 to month 48.”

“Although antibody levels decreased, up to 84.2%, 71.8%, and 76.8% of participants in the aP, wP, and EPI wP group, respectively, still possessed seroprotective levels (>0.1 IU/mL) of anti-DT IgG at 48 months of age (pre-second booster) (Table 2).”
“Similarly, 99.2%, 100%, and 100% of the participants in the aP, wP, and EPI wP group, respectively, still possessed seroprotective levels (>0.1 IU/mL) of anti-TT IgG at 48 months of age.”

“Regarding anti-Hib IgG, this study followed the kinetics of anti-Hib IgG and demonstrated a decline at months 24 and 36 (Figure 2c). Despite the decline in anti-Hib IgG levels at 24 and 36 months of age, all children in the three groups maintained seroprotection against Hib (>0.15 μg/mL) at those time points (Table 2), with over 90% achieving long-term protection (>1.0 μg/mL) (Table S6).”
“At months 24, 36 and 48, anti-PT GMC decreased over time…”

“Despite the decline in anti-DT and anti-TT IgG levels following the second booster, a greater number of children maintained seroprotective levels of anti-DT and anti-TT IgG compared to those achieved after the first booster (Tables S3 and S4).”

“Additionally, the seroprotection rate at 2 y after the second booster in our cohort remained high at >85% against diphtheria and 100% against tetanus in both pentavalent and hexavalent-vaccinated groups.”

Table 2 (seroprotection over time): Anti-DT IgG ≥0.1 IU/mL—Hexavalent (aP) group: 95.9% (24 months), 74.4% (36 months), 84.2% (48 months pre-2nd booster), 100% (49 months post-2nd booster), 95.2% (60 months), 91% (72 months); Pentavalent (wP) group: 84.1%, 56.3%, 71.8%, 100%, 93.7%, 88.5%; EPI wP group: 81.8%, 68.4%, 76.8%, 100%, 95.8%, 85.7.

Table 2 (seroprotection over time): Anti-TT IgG ≥0.1 IU/mL—Hexavalent (aP) group: 100% (24 months), 98.3% (36 months), 99.2% (48 months pre-2nd booster), 100% (49 months post-2nd booster), 100% (60 months), 100% (72 months); Pentavalent (wP) group: 100% at all timepoints; EPI wP group: 100% at all timepoints.

Table 2 (seroprotection over time): Anti-Hib IgG ≥0.15 μg/mL—Hexavalent (aP) group: 100% (24 months), 100% (36 months); Pentavalent (wP) group: 100% (24 months), 100% (36 months); EPI wP group: 100% (24 months), 100% (36 months).
key_data_points: Follow-up duration: antibody persistence assessed annually from age 2 to 6 years (DT, TT, pertussis antigens); Hib followed until age 3 years
Waning observed: anti-DT and anti-TT IgG decreased from month 19 to month 48 (pre-second booster)
Pre-second booster (48 months) diphtheria seroprotection (anti-DT IgG ≥0.1 IU/mL): 84.2% (hexavalent/aP), 71.8% (pentavalent/wP), 76.8% (EPI wP)
Pre-second booster (48 months) tetanus seroprotection (anti-TT IgG ≥0.1 IU/mL): 99.2% (hexavalent/aP), 100% (pentavalent/wP), 100% (EPI wP)
Post-second booster (49 months) diphtheria seroprotection: 100% in all groups; tetanus seroprotection: 100% in all groups
2 years after second booster (72 months) diphtheria seroprotection: 91% (hexavalent/aP), 88.5% (pentavalent/wP), 85.7% (EPI wP)
2 years after second booster (72 months) tetanus seroprotection: 100% in all groups
Hib waning: anti-Hib IgG declined at 24 and 36 months, but seroprotection (≥0.15 μg/mL) remained 100% at both timepoints in all groups
Pertussis waning: anti-PT GMC decreased over time at months 24, 36, and 48
study_population: Healthy Thai children (infants primed at 2, 4, 6 months and first booster at 18 months) randomized to hexavalent DTaP-IPV-HB-Hib (aP) vs pentavalent DTwP-HB-Hib (wP); all received Tdap-IPV second booster at 4 years; followed from age 2 to 6 years (n completed: 105 aP, 91 wP, 48 EPI wP).

evidence_snippets: “Antibody persistence in children following three doses of primary vaccination with diphtheria, tetanus, whole-cell-pertussis (DTwP), hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccines ... and response to the booster dose of DTwP-Hib (Quadrovax®) vaccine.”
“Children who completed their primary immunization were assessed for antibodies at 15–18 months of age, and then given a booster dose of DTwP-Hib vaccine.”
“Conclusions: Primary immunization with either pentavalent vaccine induced an excellent immunity lasting till the second year of life.”
“Persistence of antibodies by the two pentavalent vaccines was ascertained at the age 15–18 months.”

“Regarding Hib, suggested short-term (≥0.15 μg/ml) protection was shown by 99–100% of vaccinees in both groups. The higher antibody level (≥1.0 μg/ml), which suggests long-term protection, was slightly better (83%) in the SIIL Pentavac® than Easyfive® (76%) group.”

“For diphtheria, 90% vaccinees in both groups showed seroprotection; for tetanus the proportion of vaccinees with likely clinical protection was 89% and 87% in the SIIL Pentavac® and Easyfive® groups, respectively; for pertussis, these percentages were 49% vs. 54%, and hepatitis B 94% vs. 88%.”

“Our results re-emphasize that the SIIL-made liquid pentavalent DTwP-HB-Hib vaccine (Pentavac®) is highly immunogenic in infancy and maintains high antibody levels till the time, a booster dose is indicated.”
key_data_points: Timepoint for persistence assessment: 15–18 months of age (after 3-dose primary series at 6–10–14 weeks)
Hib seroprotection at 15–18 months: ≥0.15 μg/ml in 99–100% (both groups)
Hib ≥1.0 μg/ml (suggesting long-term protection) at 15–18 months: 83% (SIIL Pentavac®) vs 76% (Easyfive®)
Diphtheria seroprotection (≥0.1 IU/ml) at 15–18 months: 90% (both groups)
Tetanus seroprotection (≥0.1 IU/ml) at 15–18 months: 89% (SIIL Pentavac®) vs 87% (Easyfive®)
Pertussis response threshold >22 U/ml at 15–18 months: 49% (SIIL Pentavac®) vs 54% (Easyfive®)
Hepatitis B seroprotection (≥10 mIU/ml) at 15–18 months: 94% (SIIL Pentavac®) vs 88% (Easyfive®)
study_population: Indian children (infants) who previously received 3-dose primary pentavalent DTwP-HB-Hib vaccination at 6–10–14 weeks; antibody persistence assessed at age 15–18 months (n=229 enrolled; n=224 analyzed for immunogenicity).
